slides.title: Rate Limiter Overview
content: A rate limiter restricts the number of requests a client can send within a specific time period
It protects system resources and ensures stability under high traffic
Applied based on identifiers like user ID, IP address, or API key
Typically implemented at API gateway, reverse proxy, or middleware layer
Returns HTTP 429 error when request limit is exceeded

slides.title: Why Rate Limiting is Needed
content: Prevents denial of service attacks caused by excessive traffic
Protects backend systems like CPU, database, and memory
Ensures fair usage among different users
Reduces infrastructure and operational cost
Maintains predictable system latency and performance

slides.title: Basic Working Flow
content: Client sends a request to the system
System extracts identifier such as user or IP
Request count or token availability is checked
If within limit, request is processed
If limit exceeded, request is rejected with error

slides.title: Token Bucket Algorithm
content: Tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate
Each request consumes one token from the bucket
If tokens are available, request is allowed
If bucket is empty, request is rejected
Supports burst traffic while controlling average rate

slides.title: Leaky Bucket Algorithm
content: Requests are processed at a fixed constant rate
Incoming requests are stored in a queue
Requests are handled one by one at steady speed
If queue is full, new requests are dropped
Ensures smooth and predictable traffic flow

slides.title: Fixed Window Counter
content: Counts number of requests in a fixed time window
Counter resets after each time window ends
Simple and easy to implement
Allows burst at window boundaries
Boundary burst can allow more requests than expected

slides.title: Sliding Window Log
content: Stores timestamp of every request
Counts only requests within current time window
Provides highly accurate rate limiting
Requires high memory to store logs
Higher CPU cost due to timestamp processing

slides.title: Sliding Window Counter
content: Combines current and previous window counts
Reduces boundary burst problem
More efficient than sliding log approach
Provides better balance between accuracy and performance
Commonly used in real-world systems

slides.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
content: Used when multiple servers handle requests behind load balancer
Maintains shared state using centralized storage like Redis
Ensures consistent rate limiting across servers
Uses atomic operations to prevent race conditions
Enables horizontal scaling of applications

slides.title: Hot Key Problem
content: Occurs when many requests hit the same key in Redis
Overloads a single CPU core or node
Common with popular users or shared IPs
Leads to performance degradation
Requires optimization techniques to distribute load

slides.title: Handling Hot Keys
content: Use key sharding to distribute load across multiple keys
Create composite keys for better distribution
Maintain local counters for partial load handling
Implement edge rate limiting at CDN level
Balance requests across multiple storage nodes

slides.title: Hard vs Soft Limits
content: Hard limit strictly blocks requests after threshold is reached
Used in critical systems like authentication and payments
Soft limit allows small temporary bursts beyond limit
Used in less critical systems like feeds and public APIs
Choice depends on system requirements and tolerance

slides.title: Performance and Scaling
content: Deploy rate limiter across multiple data centers for resilience
Use CDN edge servers for early request filtering
Apply Redis sharding to distribute load
Use token bucket for handling burst traffic efficiently
Continuously monitor and optimize system performance

slides.title: Monitoring and Metrics
content: Track number of allowed and blocked requests
Monitor HTTP 429 responses for rate limiting effectiveness
Measure system latency and response times
Track Redis errors and performance issues
Helps adjust limits and detect system overload

slides.title: Key Concepts and Terms
content: DoS attack overloads system with excessive requests
Atomic operation ensures complete and consistent updates
Race condition occurs when multiple updates conflict
Eventual consistency means data becomes consistent over time
Burst traffic refers to sudden spikes in requests

slides.title: Final Summary
content: Rate limiter controls request flow to protect system stability
Different algorithms provide trade-offs between accuracy and performance
Distributed systems require shared state for consistent limiting
Handling hot keys and scaling is critical for large systems
Monitoring ensures proper functioning and tuning of limits
